summaries.example: Imagine making a computer weather world. The program uses rules about air, water, and heat, then moves time forward one small step at a time. It may show where a storm could go. The picture is useful, but it is still an approximation, so scientists must check how well the program works.
summaries.summary: A computer simulation is a computer-based way to study a changing system. In a narrow sense, it follows step-by-step instructions to approximate the answers to a mathematical model. In a wider sense, a simulation study includes choosing a model, writing and running code, making pictures or other displays, studying the results, and deciding what they mean. Simulations are used in weather, space science, biology, medicine, economics, and many other fields. Some use equations that describe a whole system, while agent-based simulations give separate individuals or objects their own rules. Other simulations use randomness to calculate a result. Scientists may use simulations to predict what may happen, understand patterns, or explore possibilities. Philosophers ask what kind of scientific tool a simulation is and how much trust its results deserve. A simulation may depend on approximations, computer limits, coding choices, and expert judgment, so its results need careful checking rather than automatic belief.
key_ideas: A computer simulation uses a computer to study how a system might change.
Some simulations solve or approximate equations; others use local rules for many separate agents.
Simulations can help predict, understand, or explore possible behavior.
A simulation is not automatically correct. Its choices, data, code, and approximations all matter.
Philosophers disagree about whether simulations are mainly models, experiments, methods, or scientific instruments.
summaries.why_it_matters: Simulations let scientists study systems that are too large, dangerous, slow, expensive, or difficult to test directly. They can help with questions about storms, galaxies, diseases, or groups of people. Because simulations may influence scientific conclusions and public decisions, it is important to understand both their usefulness and their limits. A colorful computer image can look like a direct observation even when it is the result of many assumptions and calculations.

important_terms.definition: A set of instructions that tells a computer what steps to carry out.
A computer-made imitation or study of a process or system.
A simpler representation used to study something more complicated.
Checking whether a simulation works well enough for its intended use.

questions_to_think_about: Why might scientists use a simulation instead of a real experiment?
What could make a computer simulation’s result less reliable?
Is a picture from a simulation the same thing as a measurement?
How might changing one rule change the result?

summaries.example: Suppose researchers simulate a severe storm. They represent the atmosphere with equations, divide space and time into small pieces, and approximate the equations on a computer. Small-scale cloud processes may be replaced by simpler parameter rules because the computer cannot represent every detail. Researchers then compare parts of the output with available observations and test how results change when resolution or assumptions change. The simulation can support a forecast, but the forecast depends on the model, code, numerical method, data, and calibration—not on computation alone.
summaries.summary:
The entry examines what computer simulations are, what they are used for, and why their scientific status is philosophically contested. In the narrow sense, a simulation is an implemented, stepwise approximation of a mathematical model. In the broader sense, a simulation study is a heterogeneous practice involving model selection, algorithm design, coding, hardware, visualization, data analysis, interpretation, and justification. This broader conception explains why simulation cannot be treated as mere calculation. Equation-based simulations use continuous theoretical equations, while agent-based simulations specify local rules for discrete entities. Multiscale simulations connect descriptions at different resolutions, and Monte Carlo methods use algorithmic randomness to calculate model properties, sometimes without mimicking a real target system.

The epistemological issue is whether simulation results are reliable enough to support claims about the world. Simulations often begin from accepted theory, but their results also depend on approximations, parameterizations, numerical techniques, engineering constraints, coding choices, and empirical calibration. They may be used where observations are sparse or direct experiments are impractical, giving them a partly autonomous role. Philosophers disagree about whether this makes simulations novel forms of modeling or experimentation, or whether they should instead be understood as methodologies or scientific instruments. Verification concerns the implementation and numerical solution; validation concerns adequacy of representation for a purpose. Yet the distinction can blur when practical computational choices affect the equations themselves. Finally, the entry discusses opacity: users may be unable to inspect all epistem7
key_ideas: Narrow definitions treat simulations as computational solvers; broader accounts include model choice, implementation, visualization, interpretation, and justification of inferences.
Equation-based, agent-based, multiscale, and Monte Carlo simulations differ in what they represent and how they calculate.
Simulation results are often downward, motley, and autonomous: they may begin with theory, depend on extra-theoretical choices, and concern cases where ordinary observation is limited.
A central dispute asks whether simulations are extensions of modeling, forms of experimentation, distinct methodologies, or scientific instruments.
Verification and validation are useful distinctions, but they may not be cleanly separable because model equations and computational methods can be adjusted together.
Complex simulations can be epistemically opaque, which creates difficult questions about reliability, trust, reproducibility, and error.
summaries.why_it_matters: Computer simulations extend what science can investigate, especially when direct intervention or observation is impossible. But their usefulness does not make their outputs self-justifying. Understanding how representations, algorithms, data, expertise, and practical constraints combine helps researchers assess claims responsibly. This matters even more when simulations guide policy, because decisions may reflect choices about what to represent, what to ignore, and which goals count as important.

important_terms.definition: A computer procedure that approximates the behavior of a mathematical model over successive steps.
A simulation in which separate entities follow local rules rather than one set of global differential equations.
The use of random steps in an algorithm to calculate properties of a model; whether it mimics a target system is debated.
Checking whether code and numerical output adequately carry out the intended mathematical procedure.
Assessing whether a model represents its target well enough for a specified purpose.
A process whose important workings are not fully accessible to the person trying to understand or use it.
The claim that results may be trusted because the process producing them tends to give reliable results, even when its inner workings are difficult to inspect.

questions_to_think_about: Does producing an unexpected simulation result make a simulation like an experiment, or can models also surprise us?
Why might verification and validation interact rather than form two independent stages?
What evidence could justify trusting an opaque simulation?
Should the standards for a precise forecast differ from those for a broad qualitative insight?
When simulations inform policy, how should modelers address assumptions and value choices?

summaries.example: A science club builds a small traffic simulation. Each car follows rules such as “slow down if the car ahead is close” and “turn at the next intersection.” After many rounds, a traffic jam appears even though no single car was told to create one. The result might help students understand how a group pattern can emerge from local rules. But they should not assume the simulation predicts a real city unless they explain why its rules and data are suitable.
summaries.summary:
Computer simulations are computer-based ways of studying systems that change. In one narrow meaning, a simulation runs step-by-step instructions to approximate the behavior described by a mathematical model. In a broader meaning, it includes the whole activity: selecting a model, translating it into an algorithm, coding it, running it, displaying the output, interpreting the data, and supporting conclusions. This broader activity involves more than mathematics because computer limits, engineering decisions, programming languages, approximations, and expert choices can affect the result.

The entry describes several kinds of simulation. Equation-based simulations use equations that describe a system globally, such as equations for a fluid or the motions of bodies. Agent-based simulations give separate agents local rules and study their interactions; these are common in social science and also appear in ecology and epidemiology. Multiscale simulations connect descriptions at different levels, while Monte Carlo simulations use randomness to calculate properties of a model. Philosophers debate whether every Monte Carlo method truly simulates a target system.

The main philosophical question is how simulations can support knowledge. Some philosophers see them as extensions of modeling, while others emphasize their similarities to experiments. Still others argue that simulations are distinctive methodologies or scientific instruments. Verification asks whether the code and numerical procedure work as intended. Validation asks whether the model is good enough for its purpose. Neither check guarantees truth by itself. Because complex simulations can be hard to inspect fully, scientists and philosophers continue to debate when their outputs deserve trust.
key_ideas: Simulations can be understood narrowly as computer calculations or broadly as complete studies involving code, data, visualization, and interpretation.
They are used for prediction, understanding, and exploration, including studying possible past causes of a present state.
Equation-based and agent-based simulations represent systems in different ways.
Philosophers disagree about whether simulations are basically models, experiments, or a separate kind of scientific practice.
A result can be mathematically well calculated but still be a poor guide to the real world if the model or assumptions are unsuitable.
The complexity of simulations makes questions about trust and checking especially important.
summaries.why_it_matters: Simulations make it possible to investigate storms, diseases, galaxies, ecosystems, economies, and other systems when direct experiments are limited. They can reveal patterns and compare possible scenarios. At the same time, a simulation’s output is shaped by its model, rules, data, code, and purpose. Learning to ask how those parts work helps us distinguish a useful scientific result from a result that only looks convincing.

important_terms.definition: A simplified representation of a real or imagined system used for investigation.
A computer process that imitates or calculates the changing behavior of another system or process.
A simulation built from equations describing how quantities change over time.
A simulation in which many separate agents follow local rules and interact.
A judgment about whether a model is suitable for the purpose for which it is being used.
A check that code and calculations perform the intended steps accurately.
Difficulty examining all the important steps by which a complex process produces its result.

questions_to_think_about: What is the difference between copying a real system and exploring a model of it?
Can a simulation teach us something if it does not exactly predict the real world?
Why might an agent-based simulation produce a group pattern that no individual agent was instructed to make?
What should scientists check before relying on a simulation?
Does a simulation count as an experiment if researchers change its inputs?
